extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, researchers of news production, and journalists interested in institutional determinants of news
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how news organizations select, gather, and construct news: the spatial placement of reporters, organizational routines, centralization via wire services, and professional practices that assign 'newsworthiness'. Useful for studying or teaching journalism sociology and newsroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations create classifications of newsworthy occurrences based on past experience; these classifications influence assignment of newsworthiness and reduce idiosyncrasy in what becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 3 and related discussion: classifications are used to sort the glut of information produced by dispersed reporters; they 'assign the attribute of ‘‘newsworthiness’’ to everyday occurrences.' The text even offers a hypothetical statistical approach (regression equation assigning numerical values to importance, significance, and interest) to illustrate objective-seeming selection methods. Use these classifications to anticipate which occurrences will be selected and how they will be framed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of reporters / geographic territoriality (beats and bureaus)
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations place reporters at specific central sites (beats, bureaus) to find occurrences that can be transformed into news stories; geographic territoriality is a principal method of dispersing reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places likely to yield news include police stations, courts, City Hall, federal courthouse, and other 'legitimated institutions.' Territorial divisions replicate an organization’s notion of its news mission and lead reporters to focus on particular localities and roles. This spatial anchoring both facilitates finding news and biases coverage toward organizations and locations that host beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of news gathering (wire services, Day Books)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wire services (Associated Press, UPI) and their products (Day Books) serve as centralized sources that connect newsrooms to occurrences worldwide and list events supposed to happen each day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire services operate as a 'spider web' linking bureaus and beats; Day Books list events that PR firms and others try to get listed to ensure coverage. Centralization reduces costs and extends reach but also produces systemic overlap and duplication among media outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: News net versus news blanket (bias toward 'big fish')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'news net' metaphor emphasizes that news-gathering systems have holes and are designed to catch certain kinds of events—usually large, institutionally-located events—rather than everything ('blanket').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A net's mesh size and investment determine what is captured: 'Today’s news net is intended for big fish.' Small-scale occurrences (e.g., a student's plagiarism) are less likely to be found than institution-level decisions. The design implies a structural bias toward occurrences at legitimated sites and toward stories with obvious organizational salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for staff-generated material over wire/service or stringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and photo/editing departments prefer work produced by their salaried staff to material from wire services or stringers, even when the external material may be superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: photography editors printing staff photos over superior wire-service pictures; television stations using their crews' footage and criticizing staff when network footage was better. Reasons include organizational investment in staff, control over bylines, and institutional loyalty. This preference reinforces the newsroom's internal hierarchies and the legitimacy of staffed beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rip-and-read (professionally frowned-upon practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small or strapped stations sometimes 'rip' copy from wire teletype and 'read' it on air verbatim without editing or localization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice is 'professionally frowned upon' and cited as indicative of resource constraints and heavy reliance on centralized services. It exemplifies an anti-pattern for original reporting and localizing news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Day Books as agenda-setting / feed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Day Books produced by wire services list planned events for a city and function as a tool by which media decide what to cover directly and what to run from wire accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-relations actors try to get events listed in Day Books to secure coverage; empirical correlation exists between Day Book listings and local media attention. Whether Day Books cause coverage or mirror independent editorial judgments can vary, but their presence exerts an agenda-setting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational routines: deadlines, rhythms, and the winnowing process
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations have objectified deadlines and work rhythms that create a glut of information which must be winnowed and classified into the news product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routines—from morning and night editions to television time slots—structure what can be covered and how material is prioritized. These routines reduce variability and encourage reliance on past experience to determine what to include; they also create incentives to recycle wire copy or copies from competitors to meet deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy and status effects on story selection (salaried reporters vs stringers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hierarchical status of information gatherers affects selection: editors prefer copy from salaried reporters whose employment represents organizational investment, whereas stringers are treated as lower-status, piecework contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice examples: bureau chiefs arguing against using stringers; stringers used only in dire need (e.g., late-night riots). This reinforces the institutional legitimacy of beat locations and dismisses 'small fish' coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic augmentation and feed dependencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic linkages (telephone cables, network feeds, rapid page transmission) connect bureaus and affiliates, enabling nearly instant sharing of copy and film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technologies supplement and sometimes duplicate reporting efforts (network feeds vs local crews). Transmission speed (e.g., 'three minutes per page') changes workflow and increases overlap among outlets, which can reinforce shared news judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stringers and attenuated relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Stringers are used to cover specialized organizations or peripheral geographic areas; their role is an attenuated relationship to the main news net.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stringers extend coverage without large investment but are associated with lower status and fewer routine opportunities; they are often used for suburbs, small colleges, or unplanned late events, affecting which stories get sustained coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: The news net's anchoring at legitimated institutions (central files and accessible information)
rubrics_metrics.description: News-gathering is anchored at institutions that maintain centralized files and official calendars, making it easier for reporters to learn about occurrences with little effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: police and fire dispatches, Board of Estimate calendars, and institutionally assembled files. Anchoring at these sites both facilitates reporting and reaffirms the public legitimacy of those institutions—occurrences there are more likely to be defined as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition and negotiation among editors/reporters shaping coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reporters negotiate and compete for assignments and bylines; these intra-newsroom and inter-editorial negotiations influence which stories are pursued and how they are placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book describes 'friendly but fierce competitors' who 'wheel and deal' to get stories printed. Understanding news requires attention to these competitive bargaining processes because they materially affect the constitution and placement of news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reportorial construction of a 'web of facticity' to maintain credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters develop methods to create a 'web of facticity'—procedures and sourcing practices intended to maintain news credibility and legitimize facts presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 5 (previewed here) emphasizes techniques reporters use to produce mutually constituting 'news sources and facts' and to legitimate certain sources while dismissing others. This process helps maintain the status quo by buttressing the credibility of selected facts and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit assumptions about readers' interests (three core assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news net presupposes three assumptions about readers: (1) interest in occurrences at specific localities, (2) concern with the activities of specific organizations, and (3) interest in specific topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions explicitly shape reporter dispersion and story selection. They justify geographic territoriality, beat assignments, and topical emphasis; questioning these assumptions reveals where and how coverage is likely to omit or marginalize certain occurrences.
